# Zelta Design

> Zelta Design is a full-service architecture firm in Nutley, New Jersey, specializing in restaurant and commercial projects. The firm has completed over 2,500 projects for +40 brands and works nationwide, licensed in 25 states and adding states as clients need them. It handles a project end to end: site survey, schematic design, construction documents, permitting and plan review, code and accessibility compliance, MEP coordination and construction administration.

## Key facts

- Legal name: Zelta Design
- Headquarters: 139 Chestnut Street, Nutley, NJ 07110
- Phone: 973-933-6636
- Email: hello@zeltadesign.com
- Principal Architect: Erik Liepins, RA (Owner)
- Licensed jurisdictions today (25): Arkansas, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Maryland, Michigan, North Carolina, Nebraska, New Jersey, New York, Ohio, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas, Virginia, Vermont, Wisconsin, West Virginia
- Service area: the United States outside California, Alaska and Hawaii. The firm gets licensed in a new state when a client brings a project there, before any drawing needs a seal.
- Completed projects: over 2,500
- Brands served: +40
- Projects published on this site: 145 (120 with photography)
- Sector focus: quick-service restaurants, fast casual, cafes, and commercial tenant fit-outs

## Guides

- [Why Your Restaurant Architect Must Be Licensed in Your State](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/architect-licensed-in-your-state/): Architects are licensed by each state, and a building department will only accept restaurant construction drawings sealed by an architect or engineer licensed in that state. An out-of-state license does not count, so a firm without a license where your site is cannot get your permit. For a multi-state rollout, the simplest path is one firm licensed in every state you are opening in.
- [Why Every Restaurant Project Starts with a Site Survey](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/existing-conditions-survey/): Restaurant drawings can only be as accurate as what is known about the space. An existing conditions survey records the real dimensions, structure and building systems before design starts, so the layout, equipment and permit set are built on facts rather than on a prototype or an old landlord drawing.
- [How Franchise Brand Design Approvals Work](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/franchise-brand-approvals/): Before a franchise location is built, the brand reviews its design in stages: a layout or test fit, then a design development set, then the documents that release the project to proceed. Brand approval is separate from the city permit. A location needs both, and a change after either approval usually has to go back through review.
- [Health Department Plan Review for Restaurants](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/health-department-plan-review/): Before a restaurant can open, the local health authority reviews its food service plans: layout, equipment, sinks, finishes, menu and food safety procedures. Who reviews them varies by state, county and town, and the packet needs as much from the operator as from the architect, so start it alongside the building drawings.
- [Opening a Restaurant in a Mall or Transit Hub: Landlord Rules](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/mall-and-transit-restaurants/): In a mall, outlet center or transit hub, the landlord reviews and approves your drawings before the town will accept a permit application, and the landlord's rules often decide your equipment, rooftop units, signage and even which trades can work on site. Read the landlord's criteria and the lease's division of work before design starts, not after.
- [Opening Many Restaurant Locations with One Architect](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/multi-unit-restaurant-rollout/): A multi-unit rollout goes faster with one architect because the brand prototype, drawing standards and permit tracking stay the same from store to store, while each site still gets its own survey, code review and permit path. The prototype is the starting point; every location is still its own building, landlord and jurisdiction.
- [Opening a Restaurant in New Jersey: Zoning, Boards and Permits](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/new-jersey-restaurant-permits/): In New Jersey, a restaurant gets zoning approval from the town first, goes to the planning board or zoning board only if the site, the use or the signs need it, then gets a construction permit under the statewide Uniform Construction Code. The local health department reviews the kitchen in parallel, and the construction official issues the certificate of occupancy after final inspections.
- [Opening a Restaurant in NYC: Permits and Approvals](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/nyc-restaurant-permits/): A New York City restaurant needs a Department of Buildings approval and work permit for the construction, filed online by a licensed architect or engineer, plus separate approvals that depend on the space: asbestos clearance, Landmarks review in historic buildings, fire department sign-offs, sign permits and the Health Department permit to operate. Most delays come from items that were not lined up before filing, not from the plan review itself.
- [Accessibility in Small Restaurants: What the ADA Requires](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-accessibility-ada/): A small restaurant has to meet two accessibility rulebooks: the federal Americans with Disabilities Act and the accessibility chapter of the building code your state adopted. In practice the entrance, the order counter, a share of the seating, the restroom and the route from parking are what get checked, and in an existing space the scope of your work decides how much else must be brought up to date.
- [Drive-thru, Inline, End-cap or Food Court: What Changes?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-building-types/): The building type decides who approves your restaurant before the building department sees it. A freestanding drive-thru answers to zoning and site plan review, an inline or end-cap unit answers to the landlord and the shell it sits in, and a food court or transit unit answers to the property owner's own review first.
- [What's in a Restaurant Construction Document Set?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-construction-documents/): A restaurant construction document set is the sealed package of drawings a building department reviews and a contractor builds from. It covers architecture plus the structural, mechanical, plumbing, electrical, sprinkler and fire alarm work the space needs, and every sheet has to agree with every other sheet.
- [Hoods, Grease and Gas: Kitchen Engineering in a Restaurant](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-kitchen-mep/): Three systems drive the engineering in a restaurant kitchen: the exhaust hood with its fire suppression and make-up air, the grease interceptor that keeps fats out of the sewer, and the gas and electric service that feeds the equipment. Each depends on the building, the landlord and the local sewer or utility, not just the drawings, so they need answers before the layout is final.
- [How Long Does It Take to Design and Permit a Restaurant?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-permit-timeline/): There is no single answer, because a restaurant is rarely one permit. Most need several separate approvals, such as building, health, zoning or fire, each with its own reviewer, order and comment cycle. The pace is set by how many approvals your site needs, which ones must come first, and how quickly comments and owner information come back.
- [Restaurant Signage: Zoning, Landlords and Historic Districts](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/restaurant-signage-permits/): A restaurant sign usually needs several separate approvals: the landlord under the lease's sign criteria, the town under its zoning sign code and sign permit, and in a historic district, a preservation commission. Sign codes vary widely, so the allowed signage should be checked before the lease is signed and the design is fixed.
- [Former Restaurant or Retail Space: Which Is Easier?](https://www.zeltadesign.com/resources/second-generation-restaurant-space/): A former restaurant, often called a second-generation space, can save time because the use, hood, grease interceptor and gas may already be there. That only helps if the equipment suits your menu, still passes inspection and the restaurant use has not lapsed. A retail conversion is a change of occupancy, so expect new kitchen infrastructure and more review.
